overview.title: Listing 4.4: the three-layer IMDb model, units, relu and sigmoid
overview.section: 4.1 Classifying movie reviews: A binary classification example
overview.main_topic: The Keras Sequential definition of the 16-16-1 sentiment model, the meaning of the number of units, and the roles of relu and sigmoid
overview.central_idea: The IMDb classifier is a keras.Sequential stack of Dense(16, relu), Dense(16, relu) and Dense(1, sigmoid). Each Dense layer computes relu(dot(input, W) + b); its unit count is the dimensionality of the representation space it projects into, a knob trading expressiveness against cost and overfitting. The sigmoid output squashes a score into [0, 1] so it can be read as the probability that a review is positive.
overview.importance: This is the canonical binary-classification architecture the book will repeat (wrap-up on p.140, review on p.625). It also introduces the idea of representation-space dimensionality as model 'freedom', which underlies the later discussion of overfitting.
learning_objectives: Read and write the Sequential model of listing 4.4
Explain what the first argument of Dense (units) controls
Derive the shape of W for each layer
Explain the trade-off of using more units
Distinguish the roles of relu (hidden layers) and sigmoid (output layer)
prerequisites: The Dense layer transformation from chapter 2 (p.77)
keras.Sequential and the MNIST example from chapters 2-3

summary:
**Figure 4.1** draws the model as three stacked boxes: input (vectorized text) -> `Dense (units=16)` -> `Dense (units=16)` -> `Dense (units=1)` -> output (probability). **Listing 4.4** is its Keras implementation, written exactly like the earlier MNIST example: `keras.Sequential([layers.Dense(16, activation="relu"), layers.Dense(16, activation="relu"), layers.Dense(1, activation="sigmoid")])`. No input shape is given; Keras infers it (10,000) the first time the model sees data.

The first argument of each `Dense` layer is its number of **units**, which the authors define as *the dimensionality of the representation space of the layer*. Recalling chapters 2 and 3, each such layer implements `output = relu(dot(input, W) + b)`. With 16 units, `W` has shape `(input_dimension, 16)`, so the dot product projects the input onto a 16-dimensional space before the bias `b` is added and `relu` is applied.

The dimensionality of the representation space can be understood as "how much freedom you're allowing the model to have when learning internal representations." More units allow more complex representations but cost more computation and can lead to learning *unwanted patterns* that help on training data but not on test data (an early hint of overfitting).

The hidden layers use `relu`, which zeroes out negative values (figure 4.2, next page); the final layer uses `sigmoid`, which squashes arbitrary values into `[0, 1]` (figure 4.3), so the output can be interpreted as the probability that the review is positive. A sidebar, **"What are activation functions, and why are they necessary?"**, begins: without a non-linearity, a `Dense` layer is just two linear operations, a dot product and an addition. The argument concludes on p.134.

concepts.name: keras.Sequential
concepts.definition: A model built from a list of layers applied in order.
concepts.intuition: A pipeline: data enters the first layer and flows through each one.
concepts.technical: Listing 4.4 passes a list of three Dense layers; the input shape is inferred at the first call.
concepts.significance: The simplest Keras model-building API, used for all of chapter 4.
concepts.misconception: You do not have to declare the input dimension here; Keras builds the weights when it first sees data.

concepts.name: Dense layer and its units
concepts.definition: A fully connected layer computing activation(dot(input, W) + b), whose first argument is the number of units.
concepts.intuition: Each unit is one learned feature detector combining all inputs.
concepts.technical: With input dimension d and u units, W is (d, u) and b is (u,).
concepts.significance: The building block of the IMDb model and of classifier heads throughout the book (p.625).
concepts.misconception: Units are not neurons laid out in space; they are just output coordinates.

concepts.name: Dimensionality of the representation space
concepts.definition: The number of dimensions of a layer's output, equal to its number of units.
concepts.intuition: "How much freedom you're allowing the model to have when learning internal representations."
concepts.technical: Higher dimension means more parameters and a larger hypothesis space.
concepts.significance: Too large invites overfitting and cost; too small creates bottlenecks.
concepts.misconception: More units are not automatically better.

concepts.name: relu
concepts.definition: Rectified linear unit, zeroing out negative values: max(0, x).
concepts.intuition: A gate that passes positive evidence and blocks negative.
concepts.technical: Piecewise linear, derivative 0 for x<0 and 1 for x>0.
concepts.misconception: Being piecewise linear, it still makes the network non-linear overall.

concepts.name: sigmoid
concepts.definition: A function that squashes arbitrary real values into the [0, 1] interval.
concepts.intuition: Turns a confidence score into a probability.
concepts.significance: Standard output activation for binary classification.
concepts.misconception: The output is not a hard 0/1 label; thresholding (e.g. at 0.5) is a separate step.

deeper.title: Counting the parameters of listing 4.4
deeper.body: Beyond the book: layer 1 has $10000\times16+16=160{,}016$ parameters, layer 2 $16\times16+16=272$, layer 3 $16\times1+1=17$; total $160{,}305$. The model is small in compute but its first layer dominates: each of the 10,000 words gets 16 learned weights, effectively a 16-dimensional word score vector summed over the words present.

deeper.title: Why a sigmoid output means a probability
deeper.body: Beyond the book: the last layer computes $z = h\cdot w + b$ (a single logit) and then $p = \sigma(z)$. Trained with binary crossentropy, $p$ is pushed toward 1 for positive reviews and 0 for negative ones, so it behaves like an estimate of $P(\text{positive}\mid\text{review})$. At inference you threshold, e.g. predict positive when $p > 0.5$, i.e. when $z > 0$.

deeper.title: Width as freedom: an analogy
deeper.body: Analogy (not in the book): asking a critic to summarize each review in 16 numbers forces them to keep only the most useful signals; allowing 1,000 numbers lets them record trivia unique to individual reviews, which helps them recall the training set but not judge new reviews. This is the 'unwanted patterns' risk the page mentions.

misconceptions.claim: The number of units in a Dense layer is its number of inputs.
misconceptions.correction: It is the number of outputs, the dimensionality of the representation space; inputs are inferred from the previous layer.

misconceptions.claim: More units always improve the model.
misconceptions.correction: The page warns they cost more compute and may learn patterns that help on training data but not test data.

misconceptions.claim: The sigmoid output is already the class label.
misconceptions.correction: It is a probability in [0, 1]; a threshold turns it into a label.

takeaways: Listing 4.4: Sequential of Dense(16, relu), Dense(16, relu), Dense(1, sigmoid).
The first Dense argument is the number of units = dimensionality of the layer's representation space.
Each hidden layer computes relu(dot(input, W) + b) with W of shape (input_dimension, 16).
More units = more freedom, but higher cost and risk of learning non-generalizing patterns.
relu zeroes negatives; sigmoid squashes to [0, 1] so the output reads as a probability.
Activation functions are needed because a Dense layer without one is only a dot product plus an addition.

questions.question: What is the shape of W in the first Dense layer of listing 4.4 when inputs are 10,000-dim multi-hot vectors?
questions.explanation: The page states W has shape (input_dimension, 16). (16, 10000) is transposed; (16, 16) is the second layer; (10000, 1) would be a layer with one unit.

questions.question: Why does the final layer use a sigmoid activation?
questions.answer: To output a single score in [0, 1] that can be interpreted as the probability the review is positive.
questions.explanation: Sigmoid squashes arbitrary values into [0, 1], suitable for a binary probability.

questions.question: According to the page, what is the risk of giving hidden layers many more units?
questions.answer: Higher computational cost and learning unwanted patterns that improve training performance but not test performance.

questions.question: What does relu do?
questions.explanation: relu(x) = max(0, x). Squashing to [0, 1] is sigmoid; summing to 1 is softmax; bias is part of the affine step.
